title: One look back
hook: he looks in on Yasodhara and the baby and does not wake them

segments.voice: Yesterday, the sleeping palace: the prince woke to see the glittering hall by plain lamplight. Your line was the spell breaks. Which room did you see with fresh eyes? Day thirty-seven.

Think of a doorway you've stood in at night. A child's room, maybe, or a parent's, or someone you loved who was sleeping. You stand there a moment longer than you need to. You don't go in. You don't say anything. You just look. The prince has decided. Tonight he will leave the palace. He has told Channa to saddle his horse. But before he goes, there is one more door he has to stand in. Down the corridor is the room where Yasodhara sleeps, with their newborn son beside her. Today, one look back.
screen: `A DOORWAY AT NIGHT.` → `THE DECISION IS MADE.` → `ONE MORE DOOR.`

segments.voice: In the later telling, he opens the door quietly. A lamp is burning. Yasodhara is asleep on a bed strewn with flowers, and her hand is resting on the baby's head. The prince stands on the threshold and wants, more than anything, to hold his son. But to lift the child, he would have to move her hand, and she would wake. And if she woke, he knew he could not go. So he stays in the doorway. The telling gives him one thought: when I have found what I'm looking for, I will come back and see my son. And he closes the door. It's one of the most tender scenes in the whole story, and it's also one people argue about. Many readers today feel the ache of it: a husband and father walking out at night without a word. Buddhists hold the story in different ways. Many see it as a great sacrifice, made for the sake of everyone, including this family. Others say plainly that it's hard, and that the tradition's honesty about the cost is part of its truth. The later stories add that Yasodhara, when she learns he has gone to live simply, gives up her own jewels and fine clothes, and that one day both she and Rahula will walk the same path. What the scene knows, whatever you make of the leaving, is how the hardest goodbyes happen. Not with speeches. In silence, from a doorway, with a hand on the frame. The Pali word for this going is nekkhamma, renunciation, and the story never pretends it's easy.
screen: `A HAND ON THE BABY'S HEAD.` · `IF SHE WAKES, HE CAN'T GO.` · `A SCENE PEOPLE HOLD DIFFERENTLY.` · `NEKKHAMMA — THE COST IS REAL.` · then, large: `THE HARDEST LEAVING IS QUIET.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably and let the breath soften. Think of a goodbye you couldn't say. Someone who left, or someone you left. A move, a breakup, a death, a friendship that just drifted. Picture them as if you were standing in a doorway, looking in. You don't need to go in. You don't need to fix anything. Just let yourself look, and let whatever you'd have said be said silently now. Then let the door close gently, and return to the breath. The bell holds the time.
One look back. The prince in the doorway, watching Yasodhara and his son asleep, choosing not to wake them.
Your line: the hardest leaving is quiet. Today, if a goodbye comes, even a small one at a door or a bus stop, let yourself look a moment longer. Day thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Buddhists tell the great going forth as the moment of renunciation, and many honor Yasodhara's part in it; the scene is often painted in temple murals, the prince standing at the door of the sleeping room.

fork.setup: you're in the doorway. your wife is asleep, her hand on your newborn son's head. you long to hold him. what do you do?
options: lift the baby gently and risk waking her.
stay in the doorway and close the door quietly.
fork.reveal: he stays on the threshold. if she woke, he could not leave, so he looks, and goes, meaning to come back.

original.note: Pali: renunciation, the going out from home life. Sanskrit naiṣkramya.

trapdoor: what you thought: the Buddha walked out on his family.
what it means: the story tells the leaving honestly, with its cost, and shows how the hardest goodbyes are made in silence.
what a scholar hears: the doorway scene is from the Nidanakatha, not the suttas; later tellings give Yasodhara her own renunciation and her own path to awakening.
